A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reward-hacking and ORPO research, despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments in four environments, including regularization comparisons, reward-hacking detection and regularization-away results (Tables 1–3 and Appendix B).

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments in the retained environments and an added RLHF setting, including reward correlations, regularization comparisons and implementation ablations (Figure 2, Table 1 and Appendix E).

M1.justification: v1 primarily optimizes proxy reward minus an occupancy KL penalty. v2 introduces a square-root χ² occupancy penalty, changing the discriminator-based reward adjustment from a linear score to an exponential score normalized by estimated divergence (Section 6 and Appendix B). It also implements direct χ² regularization for RLHF and omits v1's regularizing-away variant.

E1.justification: The tomato gridworld, Flow traffic, SimGlucose and pandemic environments remain, sometimes under renamed headings. v2 adds language-generation/RLHF experiments using AlpacaFarm preference and SFT data, substantially extending domain and task coverage (Appendix C.4).

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from KL-based AD and OM regularization to comparisons across both divergence families, including a new AD χ² comparator against χ² ORPO. The best-case early-stopping baseline in v1 Table 1 disappears. Base-policy, unregularized and true-reward-training comparisons remain for the original environments.

E3.justification: v2 introduces held-out-prompt RLHF evaluation with separate proxy and evaluation reward models, plus new χ² coefficient sweeps. Appendix D also revises the reported traffic/tomato discriminator depth from four 256-unit layers to two and specifies this architecture across non-LLM environments. Original PPO budgets remain unchanged; the revised documentation does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds proxy/true-reward correlation analyses across environments and controlled ablations of discriminator update order and reward clipping (Figure 2 and Appendix E.2). It removes v1's AUROC detection analysis and the λdrop coefficient-selection experiment. These changes substantially replace the questions investigated by the supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random seeds and median rewards with standard deviations in tables. The main coefficient-sweep plot changes from standard-deviation error bars in v1 Figure 3 to shading showing the range across seeds in v2 Figure 5. No increased repeated-run count is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds χ², RLHF, correlation and ablation results, while removing detection, early-stopping, λdrop and regularization-away results. New RLHF best-coefficient scores are 16.94 ± 0.07 for χ² and 16.81 ± 0.27 for KL. Some changed summaries reuse earlier results: gridworld AD KL changes from 6.19 to 6.33, but 6.33 already appears in v1 Table 4. Several retained appendix standard deviations also change.

T1.justification: v1's AD counterexample, TV return bound and tightness argument are replaced by correlated-proxy/reward-hacking definitions and Theorem 5.1's correlation-dependent χ² improvement bound with occupancy-support assumptions. Appendix A introduces contextual-bandit equivalence for general f-divergences, and Appendix B derives the new optimization gradient. Definition 4.1 does contain a normalization inconsistency: its stated standard deviations are printed as variances.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes OM superiority for preventing reward drops and regularizing away from hacking policies. v2 makes a new formal definition and a proxy-quality-dependent improvement guarantee central contributions, adds claims about χ² versus KL including RLHF, and recommends replacing current KL regularization. The regularizing-away contribution is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 explains hacking through breakdown of reward correlation under distribution shift and motivates χ² through its stronger penalty on unlikely behavior. It newly acknowledges that the RLHF evaluation reward model can itself be hacked and discusses limits of OM/AD equivalence for future multi-turn or tool-using agents. Earlier AUROC-based explanations and the λdrop recommendation disappear.

D1.justification: v2 adds ORPO pseudocode, a 1%-per-tail trimmed divergence estimator, proxy-reward scale values, pandemic network details, and RLHF model, dataset and software specifications. Appendix D explains previously tabulated clipping behavior but removes discriminator-training epoch counts and earlier glucose history/feature-selection guidance. These are substantive changes to implementation documentation.

R1.justification: v2 repositions the contribution around formalizing reward hacking, explicitly contrasting correlated proxies with prior unhackability and bounded-error robust-MDP formulations. It expands the distinction from offline RL and adds relevant robust-RL, RLHF and multi-turn-agent references, including Derman, Gadot and Coste. Earlier early-stopping and TV-bound supporting references are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The narrative is reorganized into preliminaries, definitions, mitigation and experiments; much ORPO derivation moves to Appendix B and environment descriptions to Appendix C. Terminology changes from safe policy to base policy, and the appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. New correlation, glucose-distribution and RLHF graphics replace earlier toy, ROC and regularization-away displays. The coefficient-sweep figure becomes separate χ²/KL rows across five environments; result tables are redesigned, and algorithm and ablation displays are added. Existing training-board and traffic illustrations remain in Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between proxy quality, a theoretical improvement bound and the implemented regularizer, addressing a limitation of v1's generic return-distance argument. New RLHF comparisons and controlled ORPO ablations add relevant empirical support and identify implementation failures. These gains outweigh losing earlier diagnostic and alternative-strategy studies, although removing the λdrop experiment weakens practical coefficient-selection evidence. Definition 4.1's normalization error and remaining discrepancies between main and appendix result summaries still require correction.
